Mikolow New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Mikołów, Poland

Not demolished. Jewish residents are first recorded in Mikołów in the 17th century; most left after the town joined Polish territory in 1922, leaving 243 Jewish residents by 1931. In 1940, the Germans transported local Jews to Sosnowiec, where most were later killed in the Holocaust. This, the newer of Mikołów's two Jewish cemeteries, was most likely founded at the beginning of the 18th century, evidenced by a recovered tombstone dated 1726, and served as the burial site for Jews of the Free State County of Pszczyna until the end of that century. The cemetery survived WWII in good condition, but on January 16, 1945, it became the execution and burial site of 14 Poles killed by the Germans, followed days later by about 50 victims of the Auschwitz-Birkenau death marches. After 1945, local residents dismantled its brick-stone wall and removed tombstones; the site briefly became a Roma encampment before its 1958 official closure. In 1988, local government cleaned and fenced the area.
